section_1.title: Geometric Interpretation of Linear Systems
section_1.content: Introduce a system of equations as the intersection of lines (in 2D) or planes (in 3D). Visualize the solution as the specific point where these geometric objects meet. Introduce the prerequisite concept: A matrix acts as a linear transformation.
section_1.example: Imagine two robots (Line A and Line B) moving on a 2D plane. Their paths are defined by 2x + y = 5 and x - y = 1. The solution is the exact coordinate (2, 1) where the robots collide.

section_2.title: Inverse Matrices: The 'Undo' Button
section_2.content: Explain that if a matrix transforms space, the inverse matrix reverses that transformation. Use a visual 'stretch/rotate' animation to show how applying A then A-inverse returns the point to its origin.
section_2.example: A 'Scale-o-matic' device doubles the size of a cat image. The inverse matrix is the 'Shrink-o-matic' that brings the cat back to its original dimensions.

section_3.title: Column Space: Where Can We Go?
section_3.content: Define Column Space as the span of the column vectors. Visually represent this as the 'territory' reachable by combining the column vectors. If the vectors are independent, they cover a plane/space; if dependent, they collapse into a line.
section_3.example: A scout dog can jump in two directions (Vector 1: North-East, Vector 2: South-East). The column space is the entire flat field the dog can reach by combining these two jump patterns.

section_4.title: Null Space: What Gets Crushed?
section_4.content: Define Null Space as the set of all vectors that result in the zero vector when multiplied by A. Visually, this is the 'shadow' or the line/plane that gets squashed into a single point (the origin) during the transformation.
section_4.example: A magical 'Flattening Lens' looks at a 3D forest. All trees standing exactly on a specific vertical line (the Null Space) are compressed into a single dot on the ground when viewed through the lens.

section_5.title: Summary and Synthesis
section_5.content: Connect the concepts: The existence of an inverse matrix implies the column space covers the entire output space and the null space contains only the zero vector (the 'no-crushing' condition).
section_5.example: If our 'Flattening Lens' (Null Space) is empty, we can perfectly reconstruct the 3D forest from the 2D image using the Inverse Matrix.
